Rationale: Well-defined NHANES cross-sectional cohort with a fully enumerated eligibility/exclusion cascade (Methods Sec. 2, Figure 1). Appropriate source population for the prediction question. The one inherent constraint -- a cross-sectional design cannot support causal claims -- is explicitly acknowledged (Methods Sec. 1, 10) rather than glossed over.

All predictors pre-specified from the literature before model building; no data-driven selection (Methods Sec. 4, with an explicit methodological argument against stepwise/LASSO selection on a fixed dataset). Skip patterns are recoded to their logical values (never-smokers as not smoking now, past-year non-drinkers as zero drinks) and refusal codes are set to missing per variable. The most incomplete predictor is LBXBSE (42.0% missing), handled with median imputation plus a missing-value indicator.

The outcome (harmonized MetS) is objectively built from lab values and treatment flags with an unusually thorough definition (Methods Sec. 3). The concern is not measurement quality but definitional sensitivity: the substituting-definition sensitivity analysis (Results Sec. 5, Table S7) shows the measured-value-only definition lowers discrimination by 0.036 to 0.037 AUROC units, and dropping the lipid-medication clause by 0.005 to 0.006, so a different defensible definition would have produced a different headline number. This is disclosed, but it is a real source of between-definition variability.

Leakage-safe pipeline (single fitted-per-fold object, Methods Sec. 6), appropriate internal cross-validation and a held-out test partition are all low-risk practices. Split-to-split variability is shown by repeated cross-validation (Table S9), and a re-tuned forward-in-time check gives AUROC 0.853 on the random split and 0.833 on the temporal holdout, calibration slope 1.06 and 1.06 (Table S10). The residual concern is that there is no external validation on an independent cohort.
